doc.title: Giacomo Gates interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, November 11, 2017 [interview 2 of 2]

title: No rehearsal and explaining the form to audiences
summary: They discuss working with unfamiliar players, telling the audience the music is fresh and not a jam session.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Yeah and the whole atmosphere of these kinds of gigs is it needs to be very relaxed for you because you are working with guys that you’ve never met before on some occasions, so you turn around and you say, “Excuse me, we’re going to rehearse.” That becomes part of that kind of gig.

And I try to let the audience know if we have a bump it’s because this is fresh. There’s no rehearsal here. We might have talked through a couple of tunes. Or, “When you get to the bridge this is going to happen okay?” But it’s not rehearsed. We didn’t spend three hours doing this prior to the gig.

I think it’s informative for people. Because a lot of times people who are not that familiar with jazz, they, one of the phrases you hear is, “Well how do they do that? How do they know to do what they’re doing?” And to actually witness a little talk-through is informative for the audience.

Yeah. I think they should know what happens. Listen this is — but, “They’re just jamming.” No they’re not. Jam is something that goes on peanut butter. This ain’t no jam session. They all know the route or the map, they all know the form, and we follow it together. So if you hear the band play something for seven minutes —
